syndromePage.intro: MED13 syndrome is a rare genetic neurodevelopmental condition associated with changes in the MED13 gene. It can affect development, speech and language, learning, and other aspects of health. Features vary from person to person.
syndromePage.populationNote: The estimate of 200 known families worldwide combines GeneDx snapshots, Simons Searchlight, the COMBINEDBrain Matrix platform, and the MED13 Foundation registry, with efforts to deduplicate. This count substantially underestimates prevalence.
syndromePage.disclaimer: Clinical features and frequency figures provide a general overview, not a prediction for any individual. Every person's experience can differ. This educational information does not replace advice from your clinician.

about.title: Who We Are
about.subtitle: Building a foundation for discovery, treatment, and hope
about.storyContent1: The MED13 Foundation was established by families directly affected by MED13 syndrome, one of the rarest neurodevelopmental disorders with just over 200 people identified worldwide. Following the first comprehensive characterization of MED13 syndrome in 2018, our community recognized the urgent need for organized advocacy and research infrastructure.
about.storyContent2: As parents navigating this ultra-rare diagnosis, we understand the isolation, uncertainty, and determination that defines this journey. We've witnessed our children's struggles with speech, learning, and development – but also their incredible resilience and unique personalities that shine through every challenge.

impact.metaDescription: A candid, denominator-aware account of MED13 Foundation's first year of research infrastructure, family participation, funding, and milestones.
impact.eyebrow: Impact and Progress · Year one, October 2025 to October 2026
impact.title: Building the evidence a MED13 treatment needs
impact.intro: When we started in October 2025, the published literature described about 28 people with MED13-related disorder. There was no longitudinal natural history data, no standard of care, and no clinical trial. This page shows what families, volunteers and partners built in our first year, and what is still needed.
impact.studyContext: Our work complements Simons Searchlight, which began collecting data on MED13 before we were founded. Ours is a patient-governed, longitudinal natural history study and biorepository. We use it to advocate for research toward treatments and to convene scientists, patients, physicians and the community.
impact.denominatorPromise: Figures are shown with numbered sources and denominators where applicable, so families, researchers and funders read the same picture.
impact.snapshot: Data as of 12 October 2026 · Updated quarterly
impact.numbersIntro: Definitions are under About these numbers, at the end of the page.
impact.metricFamiliesNote: Families enrolled, out of approximately 200 known families worldwide. Our enrolled families span six countries on four continents. The worldwide count substantially underestimates prevalence.
impact.metricFamiliesNext: Next: enroll more families. Each participant is followed over time.
impact.metricBiobankNote: Enrolled families consented to biobanking and to future research contact.
impact.metricBiobankNext: Next: multiomics pilot with imyoo on stored samples, under an approved IRB protocol.
impact.metricSurveysNote: 3 of 9 participants have at least one scored survey of adaptive function, sleep or quality of life. Rounded percentage; not completion of all required surveys.
impact.metricSurveysNext: Next: help each enrolled family complete three core measures: adaptive function, sleep and quality of life.
impact.metricEegNote: EEG files curated, of 283 that families shared from past clinical care.
impact.metricEegNext: Next: curation is part of an NIH R21 application now in review.
impact.metricCellsNote: MED13 variant classes with a disease model for assays in progress, funded by a $22,000 research grant. Models may be patient-derived or engineered.
impact.metricCellsNext: Next: our working group meets to prioritize the remaining 3 of 4.
impact.modelCapitalTitle: Disease models: committed vs. deployed capital
impact.modelCapitalNote: $56,000 committed to four models at about $14,000 each. $22,000 deployed as a research grant paid in 2026; $34,000 committed but not yet deployed.
impact.metricResearchNote: Combines $22,800 in cash research and biorepository expenses, including the $22,000 deployed disease-model grant, with $50,000 in Anthropic computing credits. Credits are in-kind resources, not deployed cash, and may not all have been used. Cash expense figures are unaudited.
impact.metricResearchNext: Next: full financial summary in our year-one impact report.
impact.fundraisingContext: Confirmed year-one support of $150,000 toward our $100,000 goal, including $50,000 in Anthropic computing credits. Credits are in-kind support, not cash donations.
impact.fundraisingNext: Next: fund the disease concept model and Mini Meeting of the MEDs.
impact.numberDefinitionNote: Study figures use the August 2026 data cut. Survey progress is 3 of 9 participants with at least one scored survey, rounded to 33%. Support and investment include in-kind credits; cash expense figures are unaudited.
impact.fitIntro: A drug developer looks for five things before working on a rare disorder. Each family that enrolls, completes a survey or donates a sample adds to the first three.
impact.fit1Body: Registry and biobank on a regulatory-grade platform.
impact.fit2Body: Natural history and outcome measures over time.
impact.fit3Body: Functional variant analysis groups variants into four classes.
impact.fit4Body: One model for assays per variant class, patient-derived or engineered.
impact.fit5Body: Assays in disease models, then clinical trials.
impact.whyFourBody: Published research suggests MED13 variants act in at least two ways. Some lower the amount of MED13 protein. Others sit in the part of the protein that controls how it is broken down. A treatment that works for one type may not work for the other, so we are building a disease model for each variant class, from patient-derived or engineered cells, for use in assays.
impact.roadmapIntro: Our path follows the stages other rare disease foundations have used from founding to clinical trials. Of 21 milestones, 5 are done, 6 are in progress and 1 is next.
impact.stage3Years: Years 4 to 5 · 2028 to 2030 · one milestone started early
impact.m1Title: Launch patient registry and biorepository enrollment
impact.m1Detail: Live since January 2026 on the COMBINEDBrain Matrix platform, which meets HIPAA, GDPR and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 requirements. 9 participants in 6 countries.
impact.m2Detail: Our Scientific and Clinical Advisory Board held its first meeting on 9 September 2026.
impact.m3Detail: Monthly virtual family meetup led by a parent volunteer, spring and summer family newsletters, and a relaunched med13.org.

impact.m4Detail: Incorporated in California in October 2025. COMBINEDBrain member. Fiscally sponsored by Rare Village Foundation. Next: adopt governance policies and file our own 501(c)(3) application.
impact.m5Detail: $22,000 deployed as a research grant paid in 2026 for stem cell line generation and quality control. This is part of the $56,000 committed to four disease models, not an additional amount.

impact.m6Detail: MEDopathies Virtual Scientific Symposium on MED12, MED13 and MED13L, with a family panel, 9 October 2026. Next: in-person Mini Meeting of the MEDs in Denver, December 2026.
impact.m7Detail: Collecting standard measures of adaptive function, sleep, behavior and quality of life, and developing patient-centered comparative effectiveness research (CER) questions for a PCORI application. An NIH R21 on EEG-based trial design is in review.
impact.m8Detail: Analyzing how MED13 variants change protein function, so each variant can be interpreted and grouped by mechanism.
impact.m10Title: Commission Strategic Research Plan and disease concept model
impact.m10Detail: A family-informed research roadmap and a disease concept model, planned for 2027. The disease concept model has a $10,000 funding need.

impact.m13Detail: Depends on disease models across variant classes.
impact.m14Detail: Depends on knowing which mechanism each variant class follows.
impact.m16Detail: Enrolling now. The study is longitudinal: each participant is followed over time.

impact.step1Body: Disease models: Our working group and the Scientific and Clinical Advisory Board prioritize the next 3 of 4 disease models.
impact.step3Body: Biomarker pilot: Pilot multiomics with imyoo on biorepository samples under an approved IRB protocol.

Completing your surveys helps advance study progress; 3 of 9 participants currently have at least one scored survey.
impact.researchersBody: Refer families, request de-identified data through COMBINEDBrain under a data use agreement, or propose a study on the disease models or EEG records.
impact.donorsBody: Help fund the disease concept model ($10,000) and the Mini Meeting of the MEDs in Denver, December 2026 ($7,000). These funding needs are separate from the $56,000 already committed to disease models. Ask us for the year-one impact report.
impact.aboutIntro: Research progress is not a promise of a treatment. These definitions and limits are part of the record.
impact.definition1: Study figures come from the natural history study data cut of August 2026. Survey progress is the share of participants with at least one scored survey: 3 of 9, or 33% rounded to the nearest whole percent. It does not measure completion of every required survey. Other small-cohort figures are reported as counts. Nothing on this page should guide any individual's medical care.
impact.definition2: Approximately 200 known families worldwide is a combined estimate from GeneDx snapshots, Simons Searchlight, the COMBINEDBrain Matrix platform, and the MED13 Foundation registry. We make efforts to deduplicate across these sources. This count substantially underestimates prevalence; it is not a measured prevalence estimate. The nine enrolled participants represent nine separate families.
impact.definitionGeneticIncidence: GenIE, the Broad Institute's Genetic Prevalence and Incidence Estimator, estimates that new disease-causing MED13 variants arise in about 1 in 82,000 births (1.216 per 100,000). This is a modeled estimate from gnomAD and ClinVar, not a count of diagnosed people, and suggests many people are undiagnosed.
impact.definition3: The four variant classes are truncating variants, missense variants in the region that controls protein breakdown, missense variants in a recurrent hotspot, and other missense variants.
impact.definitionCapital: Committed capital is funding the foundation has pledged to disease models; deployed capital is funding already paid. The October 2026 commitment totals $56,000 for four models at about $14,000 each, with $22,000 deployed and $34,000 not yet deployed. The report's cost estimate includes blood draw, multiomics and iPSC generation. A paid grant does not mean a model is complete. The $22,000 is already included in the $22,800 of cash research expenses; these figures must not be added together.
impact.definition4: Cash expense figures cover 1 January to 10 October 2026 and are unaudited: $22,800 of $38,360 in total expenses went to research grants and the biorepository. Funds are held by our fiscal sponsor, Rare Village Foundation (EIN 83-4699994). The foundation confirmed $150,000 in year-one support against a $100,000 goal, including $50,000 in Anthropic computing credits. Research investment combines $22,800 in cash research expenses with those same credits; the credits are not additional fundraising or deployed cash, and their inclusion does not imply they have all been used. The $34,000 committed but not yet deployed is not included as cash spending or added to research investment.
impact.definition5: MED13 Foundation is a California nonprofit public benefit corporation preparing its own application for 501(c)(3) recognition.
impact.fiscalBody: MED13 Foundation operates as a fiscally sponsored project of Rare Village Foundation (EIN 83-4699994), a 501(c)(3) public charity. Gifts made through Rare Village Foundation are tax-deductible to the extent allowed by law. MED13 Foundation is preparing its own application for 501(c)(3) recognition.

events.storiesAndEssaysSubtitle: Personal reflections from the MED13 community
events.reflectionParagraph1: When I started MED13.org, I never anticipated families reaching out with questions about their unborn children. The first time this happened, a diagnostic company reached out to me indirectly. I diligently contacted all of our board members, studied the variant, spoke with a medical ethicist and clinical geneticist, and responded to the diagnostic company that they could put me in touch with the family directly but that, honestly, there are more unknowns than knowns about MED13 at this time and each person diagnosed is helping us to understand the full spectrum of disease, from fatal to silent. I imagine this is also true of the other 10,000 and counting rare monogenetic diseases that we currently diagnose. The response: silence.
events.reflectionParagraph2: The second time this came up, I was no more prepared. I had taken a week off to be with my children during a school break and came back to a message titled “Prise de contact.” I don’t speak French, but I could tell this was urgent and it had been sent five days earlier. I offered the standard meet and greet, but the mother replied that they had already decided to send their child to the stars. I was shocked. Had I misinterpreted this? What could I have done? I asked for clarification, and she shared that the abortion was planned for Friday. It was Tuesday at midnight. I immediately contacted all of the experts who could tell me anything about this variant and learned that, in all likelihood, it was pathogenic. But the truth is that we don’t know how it would present. I did set up the call with the mother and a French woman who agreed to translate for us. As I prepare for the meeting, I am aware that all I can do is listen, share our own story, what we are hearing from other families, and the lack of evidence in the literature. There are so many unknowns, and I certainly did not anticipate receiving these types of emails when I started this journey a year ago, but I am grateful that we can be a place where parents can come to ask questions today and hope for the future.

events.constellationMetaphor: In this campaign, each child is a star and our whole community is The Constellation. We are all aboard one small blue boat, finding our way by each other’s light and steering toward the North Star: better treatments and good days along the way.
events.constellationDignity: A star does not have to do anything to shine; it shines simply by being.

events.starOfMonthSeptemberImageAlt: Xander smiling while sitting on playground equipment
events.starOfMonthSeptemberJourney1: Xander is a happy, easygoing boy. He spent his first 22 days in the NICU. He was diagnosed with MED13 at 9 months old after being followed during pregnancy for abnormal brain imaging and showing signs of developmental delays.
events.starOfMonthSeptemberJourney2: At 2½ years old, Xander participates in intensive therapies and is working on standing at a surface, transitioning from lying to sitting, walking with a gait trainer, and using eye-gaze technology. He works hardest for Super Simple Songs and snacks.
events.starOfMonthSeptemberClosing: Xander is showing more interest, attention, and understanding. He has a silly sense of humor, communicates what he wants without words, and is beginning to follow simple directions.
events.starOfMonthImageAlt: Arturo smiling in a purple amusement park ride
events.starOfMonthLove2: His big sister Anna Sofia (6), and imitating everything she says and does
events.starOfMonthLove4: Calling family and friends on FaceTime
events.starOfMonthLove5: Reading books and listening to stories
events.starOfMonthJourney1: Arturo was born small in January 2023 and did not grow because of severe dysphagia. When his parents noticed that his eyes were not focusing, a neuro-ophthalmologist ordered genetic testing and an MRI. After recurring lung infections, surgeries, diagnostic biopsies, and many hospital stays, Arturo was diagnosed with MED13 at age 1. He is on the autism spectrum, has global developmental delays, and has cortical visual impairment.
events.starOfMonthJourney2: He is able to grow and thrive with a G-tube, speech, occupational, physical, and hippotherapy, as well as an aide who helps him participate in his community preschool.
events.starOfMonthClosing: Arturo is very social and loves to greet everyone he meets with a smile and a song.

symposium.liveTranslation: Live translation will be available via Zoom for the symposium.
symposium.openAccessNote: Save the date · Registration details will be published soon.
symposium.eventCardDesc: A full day of research presentations, panels, and family perspectives across MED12, MED13, and MED13L.
symposium.whyTitle: One module. Three genes. One community.
symposium.whyBody1: MED12, MED13, and MED13L are regulatory subunits of a single molecular machine: the CDK8 kinase module of the Mediator complex, the switchboard every cell uses to turn genes on and off during brain development.
symposium.whyBody2: The three disorders share structure, overlapping clinical features, and a set of open scientific questions. This symposium is the MEDopathies Alliance’s first public program: one module, three genes, one community.
symposium.programNote: All times are Pacific. The full speaker list will be published with the final program.
symposium.session1Title: Welcome: the case for the MEDopathies Alliance
symposium.session1Description: A brief joint opening from the leaders of the three foundations.
symposium.session1Speakers: Amy Krystosik, PhD, MPH, MED13 Foundation · Katie Barry Boychuck, MED13L Foundation · Kelly Sarber, MED12 Foundation
symposium.session2Title: The Mediator complex and the CDK8 kinase module
symposium.session2Description: Cryo-EM of the human Mediator kinase module and the structural target landscape, with emphasis on the distinction between MED13 and MED13L. Followed by audience Q&A.
symposium.session2Speakers: Dr. Kuang-Lei Tsai, UTHealth Houston · introduced and moderated by Dr. Dylan Taatjes, University of Colorado Boulder
symposium.session3Title: Model systems across the Mediator spectrum
symposium.session3Description: One module, three genes, one open question: what each model system can and cannot tell us, where the three disorders converge, and where they do not.
symposium.session3Speakers: Zexuan Li, UC Santa Cruz · Dr. Maya Arce, Arc Institute · Julie McMurry, MPH, UNC Chapel Hill · moderated by Dr. Dylan Taatjes
symposium.session4Title: Natural history, phenotype, and cohort readiness
symposium.session4Description: What we know about the course of these disorders, and how registries and biorepositories make the cohort trial-ready.
symposium.session4Speakers: Dr. Alana Strong, Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) · Dr. Carla Marini, Salesi Children’s Hospital · Maya Chopra, MBBS, FRACP, Boston Children's Hospital / Harvard Medical School · Lindsay Wieczorek, COMBINEDBrain · moderated by Terry Jo Bichell, COMBINEDBrain
symposium.session5Description: MED13L includes well-documented dosage loss and missense variants of unresolved mechanism. MED13 carries both truncating and missense variants. Until we can assign a mechanism class variant by variant, we cannot honestly tell a family which therapeutic path is theirs.
symposium.session5Speakers: Dr. Ryan L. Boudreau, University of Iowa · Dr. Nadav Ahituv, UCSF · Dr. Wayne Poon, NeuCyte · moderated by Ricardo N. Ramirez, PhD, MED13L Foundation
symposium.session6Description: How ultra rare programs get built and funded. 10 min talk, 5 min Q&A.
symposium.session9Title: Building the healthcare system for generations of patients with genetic diseases
symposium.session9Description: Connecting fragmented research and data efforts so advances in genetic medicine reach patients faster. 10 min talk, 5 min Q&A.
symposium.session9Speakers: Mimi Lee, MD, PhD · Founder, Opus 132
symposium.session7Title: Living with a disorder of this module
symposium.session7Description: A conversation among parents from all three communities: two families each from MED12, MED13, and MED13L, invited by their own foundation. This session is recorded for the communities but excluded from the open license, and every panelist retains the right to withdraw.
symposium.session7Speakers: Moderated by Jean Chia, MD, Stanford Medicine Children’s Health
symposium.session8Description: What comes next: the MEDopathies Research Workshop in Denver in December 2026 alongside the AES Annual Meeting, and the Meeting of the MEDs in June 2027.
symposium.session8Speakers: Amy Krystosik, PhD, MPH, MED13 Foundation · Katie Barry Boychuck, MED13L Foundation · Kelly Sarber, MED12 Foundation
symposium.speakersTitle: The people moving the field forward
symposium.speakersIntro: The full speaker list will be published with the final program.
symposium.speaker1Affiliation: Associate Professor, Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, McGovern Medical School, UTHealth Houston
symposium.speaker1Bio: Internationally recognized for pioneering structural work on the Mediator complex and its CDK8 kinase module, including studies that uncovered the critical role of the MED13 subunit in regulating Mediator activity. His laboratory uses cryo-electron microscopy with biochemical and biophysical approaches to understand how transcriptional dysregulation contributes to human disease.
symposium.speaker2Affiliation: Professor, Biochemistry, University of Colorado Boulder
symposium.speaker2Bio: The Taatjes lab studies the molecular mechanisms that control human gene expression, focusing on the Mediator complex within the transcription pre-initiation machinery, and how transcription and signaling pathways are altered in development and disease.
symposium.speaker3Affiliation: Director, Pediatric Neuropsychiatry Unit, Salesi Children’s Hospital, Ancona, Italy
symposium.speaker3Bio: A pediatric neurologist and internationally recognized expert in pediatric epilepsy, neurogenetics, and developmental epileptic encephalopathies, with more than 300 peer-reviewed publications contributing to the discovery of disease-causing genes and precision medicine in neurological disorders.
symposium.speaker4Bio: Leads an Arc Institute group using large genomic datasets and CRISPR screening to understand how gene variation affects immune cell function. During her PhD at UCSF in the Alex Marson Lab, her first-author Nature study showed how MED12 acts as a central coordinator of dynamic gene circuits governing T-cell rest and activation.
symposium.speaker5Bio: His laboratory links gene regulatory elements and their variation to human disease, and pioneered cis-regulation therapy: using regulatory elements as therapeutic targets for haploinsufficiency disorders. His team recently demonstrated CRISPR activation as a rescue of SCN2A haploinsufficiency in mouse and human stem-cell-derived neurons.
symposium.speaker6Bio: A neuroscientist and former public health nurse-midwife who launched COMBINEDBrain in 2019, a pre-competitive consortium of patient advocacy organizations working to identify outcome measures and biomarkers for rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders. She earned her PhD in neuroscience from Vanderbilt and came to this work as the parent of a son with Angelman syndrome.
symposium.speaker7Affiliation: Chief Scientific Officer and Biorepository Director, COMBINEDBrain
symposium.speaker7Bio: A biomedical scientist and rare disease advocate with over 20 years of experience across immunology, infectious disease, and neurodevelopmental research. Previously Scientific Director of the Synap Research Fund, she led real-world data initiatives for drug repurposing and co-directed the Humoral Immunology Section at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research.
symposium.speaker8Bio: A genome and data science leader with deep expertise in epigenetics, computational biology, immunology, and gene-editing technologies. As CSO of the MED13L Foundation, he leads investigational research and preclinical strategy toward viable therapies for MED13L syndrome.
symposium.speaker9Affiliation: Acting Director, Division of Rare Diseases Research Innovation, NCATS, National Institutes of Health
symposium.speaker9Bio: Leads NCATS’ rare disease research division and represents NCATS in the NIH-wide Gene Therapy Working Group and the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium. He is co-coordinator of the NIH Common Fund program on Somatic Cell Genome Editing and co-chair of the Bespoke Gene Therapy Consortium.
symposium.speaker10Affiliation: Clinical Assistant Professor, Pediatrics, Stanford Medicine Children’s Health
symposium.speaker10Bio: A board-certified pediatrician caring for children with medical complexity at Stanford Medicine Children’s Health’s Complex Primary Care Clinic. Trained at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine with pediatric residency at NYU, she brings a clinician’s perspective to conversations between families, researchers, and care teams.
symposium.speaker11Affiliation: PhD student, Molecular, Cell & Developmental Biology, UC Santa Cruz
symposium.speaker11Bio: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental disorders. His first-author study in Communications Biology demonstrated that Med13 regulates cortical neuron radial migration and contralateral projection through the PlxnA4 signaling pathway, providing new mechanistic insight into MED13-associated disorders.
symposium.speaker12Affiliation: Professor, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
symposium.speaker12Bio: Directs TISLab, an interdisciplinary team of data scientists, software engineers, and domain experts building the software and integrative data stack behind rare disease diagnosis and research. She has led international efforts on persistent identifiers, data citation, and cross-species phenotype integration, including Monarch Initiative work that harmonizes genotype-phenotype data across model organisms and patients, and the 44-author "Identifiers for the 21st century" paper (PLoS Biology, 2017).
symposium.speaker13Bio: A physician and biomedical innovation leader working to build shared infrastructure for rare and genetic disease research. She conceived, designed, and launched THRIVE, a $160M program at ARPA-H focused on embedding patient voices in program design and extending breakthrough therapies to communities beyond major academic centers. Through Opus 132 she works to connect fragmented research and data efforts so that advances in genetic medicine reach patients faster.
symposium.speaker14Affiliation: Attending Physician, Division of Genetics & Genomics, Boston Children's Hospital; Assistant Professor of Neurology, Harvard Medical School
symposium.speaker14Bio: A clinical geneticist and pediatrician who directs Translational Genomic Medicine at the Rosamund Stone Zander Translational Neuroscience Center, where her work centers on discovering and delineating rare monogenic neurodevelopmental syndromes and evaluating which disorders are suited to gene-based therapies and ready for clinical trials. She co-authored the consensus guidelines on assessing variant eligibility for antisense oligonucleotide treatments and the GENE TARGET framework for evaluating neurodevelopmental disorders for gene therapy, and she leads multidisciplinary clinics that connect diagnosis to therapeutic strategy.
symposium.accessTitle: Open science, with room for family choice
symposium.openBody: Keynotes and scientific sessions are recorded and posted publicly under CC BY 4.0, together with short edited clips of the keynotes and panels.
symposium.familyBody: Hosted by the Alliance, all rights are reserved and revocable at any time by any panelist. An open license is irrevocable, so we choose the right to withdraw.
symposium.privacyBody: Because sessions are posted publicly, no session displays individual-level genotype-phenotype tables, clinical photographs, or other identifiable data.
symposium.recordingNote: Sessions are recorded for public access after the event. Family participants retain the right to withdraw from their session.

whoWeAre.heroSubtitle: Parents, professionals, and scientists working together to change what a MED13 diagnosis means
whoWeAre.heroIntro: The MED13 Foundation is parent-led and family-driven. We are building the research tools that will enable treatments, and connecting every family who needs us.
whoWeAre.storyContent1: When our son was diagnosed with MED13 syndrome in 2024, there was no foundation, no research cohort, and almost no infrastructure to find other families like ours. MED13 syndrome was first described in the medical literature in 2018. The entire history of this diagnosis fits within a few years.
whoWeAre.storyContent2: In October 2025, we officially launched the MED13 Foundation. The foundation was co-founded by families of children with MED13, drawing on backgrounds in epidemiology, disease research, and data infrastructure from institutions like Stanford and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.
whoWeAre.storyQuote: We decided not to wait for the research to find us. We decided to build the infrastructure that would make research possible.
whoWeAre.boardSubtitle: A dedicated board of parents, professionals, and advocates
whoWeAre.sabSubtitle: World-class scientists spanning brain organoids, molecular mechanisms, and clinical genetics
whoWeAre.openingsText: We are actively searching for dedicated and motivated board members to contribute their skills. If you'd like to help build the future for MED13 families, we'd love to hear from you.
whoWeAre.fundersSubtitle: We are grateful to the organizations investing in MED13 research and the rare disease community
whoWeAre.anthropicDescription: The MED13 Foundation was awarded $50,000 in Claude credits through Anthropic’s AI for Science rare disease research grants program. This support expands our capacity to use AI in service of MED13 research and the broader rare disease community.
whoWeAre.anthropicThanks: Thank you, Anthropic, for supporting patient-led rare disease research and helping move MED13 science forward.
whoWeAre.anthropicLinkLabel: Read Anthropic’s rare disease research grants announcement
whoWeAre.partnersSubtitle: We are grateful to the organizations who have welcomed the MED13 Foundation into their networks
whoWeAre.director3Bio: Co-founder of Audity AI and RAC Projects AI, where he builds AI-powered frameworks that help businesses diagnose readiness and move from strategy to implementation. He brings a decade of financial and business development experience from JPMorgan Chase, where he was a Presidents Club achiever managing $15M+ in annual new client business. He holds a certificate in IoT Product Development from Stanford Continuing Studies.
whoWeAre.director2Bio: Biomedical Informatics Data Scientist at Stanford Health Care, working at the intersection of clinical research data and applied AI. His work focuses on LLM evaluation, agent systems, and building dependable AI workflows for regulated environments, including natural-language interfaces for clinical cohort discovery and governed pipelines with human review and audit trails. He brings ten years of experience delivering clinical databases, data pipelines, and analytics tools for research teams.
whoWeAre.director4Bio: Chairman of the Executive Board at Lone Star Abilities Network, where she advocates for individuals with disabilities through programs that expand opportunity and quality of life. She co-founded Frisco SAGE and the Frisco Gifted Association, providing advocacy and programming for families of academically gifted students, including those who are twice-exceptional. Her background in educational psychology and non-profit leadership drives her commitment to inclusive community impact.
whoWeAre.director5Bio: Seasoned program professional with a strong track record leading complex technology initiatives through contract management, team development, and strategic delivery. She brings expertise in risk assessment, information security, and incident management, and holds a Master's in Information and Telecommunications Systems from Johns Hopkins University.
whoWeAre.director7Bio: Director of Family Education and Engagement at Courageous Parents Network, where she advocates for families navigating pediatric palliative and hospice care. A client success and program management professional, she brings experience leading complex workflows, stakeholder partnerships, and education initiatives across healthcare and nonprofit settings, with a focus on improving adoption, satisfaction, and outcomes.
whoWeAre.director7Role: Nonprofit Director · Pediatric Palliative Care Advocate
whoWeAre.staffSubtitle: The people working day-to-day alongside our families
whoWeAre.staff2Bio: Virologist and Research Scientist at Stanford University School of Medicine, leading interdisciplinary studies on infectious disease epidemiology and virus evolution. She is currently collaborating with the Gates Foundation on a project to develop a safer poliovirus vaccine to reach eradication. Izabela holds a PhD in Microbiology/Virology from the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, as well as a Master's in Infectious Diseases and a B.S. in Biology from the Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora. At the Foundation, she helps plan events and manages the CRM.
whoWeAre.advisor1Role: UC San Diego · Gene Therapy Initiative · Brain Organoids
whoWeAre.advisor2Role: Rowan University · MED13L/Cyclin C Molecular Mechanisms
whoWeAre.advisor3Role: Rowan University · MED13L/Cyclin C Molecular Mechanisms
whoWeAre.advisor5Role: Karolinska Institute · Professor of Clinical Genetics
whoWeAre.advisor6Role: University of Colorado Boulder · Professor of Biochemistry · Mediator Complex Biochemistry
whoWeAre.advisor7Role: Former CZI Science (Rare As One) · Funder Strategy & Philanthropy
whoWeAre.cabSubtitle: Treating clinicians guiding care and clinical research for MED13 families
whoWeAre.clinician1Role: Director of Child Neuropsychiatry · G. Salesi Children's Hospital, Ancona, Italy · Pediatric Epilepsy
whoWeAre.advisor8Role: UTHealth Houston · Associate Professor of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology
whoWeAre.director1Bio: Epidemiologist and data scientist who became a rare-disease founder after her son's MED13 diagnosis. She founded the MED13 Foundation in 2025 to build the infrastructure families need to reach emerging therapies, including a biorepository, natural-history registry, and clinical protocols developed through COMBINEDBrain. She previously spent six years as a data scientist at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and a decade building global health research cohorts. PhD in Epidemiology; MPH in international health and development; postdoctoral training in pediatric infectious disease epidemiology and community health at Stanford School of Medicine.
whoWeAre.director6Bio: C-suite technology leader with over two decades in enterprise IT strategy, cybersecurity oversight, and digital innovation across Saudi Arabia and international markets, spanning sectors from banking and government to health and retail. His youngest daughter's diagnosis with MED13 syndrome inspired him to champion care and advocacy for affected families. He contributes to patient advocacy, research acceleration, and biorepository development at the MED13 Foundation.
whoWeAre.director8Bio: Mom to a son with MED13-related syndrome and an expert at navigating therapies and healthcare providers. Passionate about research and advocacy, she also works in product management in the healthcare technology space. She lives in North Carolina with her husband Jon and two boys.
whoWeAre.staff1Bio: Family Liaison for the MED13 Foundation, working alongside families enrolled in the MED13 Natural History Study to guide them through the research process, answer questions, and connect them with opportunities to contribute. She believes rare disease research is strongest when families are true partners, and is committed to ensuring every family feels heard, supported, and empowered.
whoWeAre.advisor2Bio: Research Program Coordinator at the Brown Virtual Integrated Special Needs Center. Her doctoral work centered on mitochondrial structure and cellular membrane composition dynamics. She focuses on translational research and researcher-clinician-advocate collaborations.
whoWeAre.advisor3Bio: Molecular cell biologist studying the fundamental cellular mechanisms relevant to rare disease, bringing bench-science depth to the alliance's scientific program.
whoWeAre.advisor4Bio: Clinical geneticist focused on the diagnosis and characterization of rare neurodevelopmental disorders, contributing European clinical and genomic expertise.
whoWeAre.advisor5Bio: Senior clinical geneticist at Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, specializing in rare genetic disorders and rare disease gene discovery and diagnostics.
whoWeAre.advisor6Bio: Leads a lab defining the architecture and function of the Mediator complex and its CDK8 kinase module, the machinery at the center of the Medopathies. His landmark discovery established foundational links in the gene transcription disrupted across all three MEDopathy genes.
whoWeAre.advisor7Bio: Neuroscientist and scientific strategist with 25+ years of experience launching and growing scientific initiatives. Founder of Lark Science Advisors; formerly Neuroscience Program Lead at Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, where she established the Neurodegeneration Challenge Network and helped develop the N=1 Collaborative, which strengthened partnerships between researchers and patient organizations. Previously Editor-in-Chief of Neuron at Cell Press.
whoWeAre.advisor8Bio: Associate Professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at McGovern Medical School, UTHealth Houston. Internationally recognized for pioneering cryo-EM studies on the structure and function of the Mediator complex, including the critical role of the MED13 subunit in regulating Mediator activity, and how alterations in this complex contribute to human disease.
whoWeAre.advisor9Role: TISLAB, UNC · Monarch Initiative · Precision Health & Data Infrastructure
whoWeAre.advisor9Bio: Director of precision health and translational informatics at UNC and co-founder of the Monarch Initiative. She builds the data and ontology infrastructure that helps rare diagnoses get recognized, studied, and linked to mechanism, making it possible for researchers to find and connect the patients who need them.
whoWeAre.clinician1Bio: Internationally recognized pediatric neurologist and expert in epilepsy and neurogenetics. She earned her PhD at the University of Melbourne under Prof. Samuel Berkovic, has authored more than 300 publications (H-index 66), and directs the Pediatric Neuropsychiatry Unit at Salesi Children's Hospital. She is collecting MED13 samples and co-authoring the MED13 GeneReview.
